section: Problem 4: Counting parameters for five variables
text:
Problem 4: Counting parameters for five variables
Take N=5 binary variables x_1,\dots,x_5. Using the chain rule in the order x_1,\dots,x_5 with no assumptions, how many parameters does the factorization need?
Now suppose we are willing to assume x_5 depends only on x_2 and x_4 (not on x_1 or x_3), while every other factor stays as general as before. How many parameters does the factorization need now, and how many were saved?






TipWorked solution





This uses Week 2, Free parameters and the cost of the full joint and Why factor the joint.
With no assumptions, the chain rule gives p(x_1)p(x_2\mid x_1)p(x_3\mid x_1,x_2)p(x_4\mid x_1,x_2,x_3)p(x_5\mid x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4). Each factor p(x_j\mid x_1,\dots,x_{j-1}) needs 2^{j-1} parameters, so the totals are 1,2,4,8,16 for j=1,\dots,5, summing to 1+2+4+8+16=31, matching 2^5-1=31 exactly.
Replacing the last factor with p(x_5\mid x_2,x_4) shrinks its table from 2^4=16 parameters (one per configuration of four parents) to 2^2=4 (one per configuration of two parents). The new total is 1+2+4+8+4 = 19.
Savings: 31-19=12 parameters, all from dropping x_5’s dependence on x_1 and x_3. This is the same pattern as the lecture’s N=4 example: dropping dependence on conditioning variables shrinks that one factor’s table exponentially, and the saving compounds because that factor was the largest one in the sum.
Answer. No assumptions: 31 parameters. With x_5\mid x_2,x_4: 19 parameters. Savings: 12.

section: Problem 5: CPT sizes for an invented graph
text:
Problem 5: CPT sizes for an invented graph
Consider a DAG on five binary nodes y_1,\dots,y_5 with edges y_1 \to y_2, y_1 \to y_3, y_2 \to y_4, y_3 \to y_4, y_4 \to y_5 (so y_4 has two parents, y_2 and y_3).
For each node, state its parent count K_i and its CPT size 2^{K_i}. Sum these to get the total number of parameters, and compare to the 2^5-1 a fully-connected DAG on five nodes would need.






TipWorked solution





This uses Week 2, Directed graphical models.
Read the parent count off the incoming edges at each node:

y_1: no parents, K=0, CPT size 2^0=1.
y_2: one parent (y_1), K=1, CPT size 2^1=2.
y_3: one parent (y_1), K=1, CPT size 2.
y_4: two parents (y_2,y_3), K=2, CPT size 2^2=4.
y_5: one parent (y_4), K=1, CPT size 2.

Total: 1+2+2+4+2 = 11 parameters, against 2^5-1=31 for the fully-connected case on five nodes. The saving comes from every node having at most two parents instead of depending on every node before it; y_4’s CPT is the largest single piece because it is the only node with two parents.
Answer. K = (0,1,1,2,1), CPT sizes (1,2,2,4,2), total 11 parameters, versus 31 fully connected.

title: Week 2 practice: Decision theory and graphical models
section: Problem 6: Chain, common cause, or collider?
text:
Problem 6: Chain, common cause, or collider?
Three sensors on a machine: a temperature reading (X), an internal wear level (Y), and a vibration reading (Z). Consider this causal story: high internal wear (Y) tends to raise both the temperature reading (X) and the vibration reading (Z), but the temperature and vibration sensors do not affect each other directly: X \leftarrow Y \rightarrow Z.
Which of the lecture’s three canonical structures is this? Are X and Z independent before observing Y? What happens once Y (the wear level) is observed?






TipWorked solution





This uses Week 2, Conditional independence: three canonical structures.
This is the common cause structure, X \leftarrow Y \rightarrow Z, with wear level Y as the shared cause of both readings.
Marginally (before observing Y), X and Z are dependent: a high temperature reading is evidence of high wear, which in turn makes a high vibration reading more likely, so the two readings move together even though neither sensor affects the other. This is the same “two effects of a shared cause are correlated” pattern as the lecture’s deadline example.
Once Y is observed, the joint factors as p(y)p(x\mid y)p(z\mid y), so p(x,z\mid y) = p(x\mid y)p(z\mid y): conditioning on the wear level uses up the shared explanation, and X \perp Z \mid Y. Knowing the wear level directly, the temperature reading tells us nothing more about the vibration reading.
Answer. Common cause. X and Z are marginally dependent, and become conditionally independent given Y: X \perp Z \mid Y.

title: Week 2 practice: Decision theory and graphical models
section: Problem 7: Bayes Ball on a small graph
text:
Problem 7: Bayes Ball on a small graph
Consider a DAG with edges p \to q, r \to q, q \to s, r \to t (so q is a collider with parents p and r, and r also has a second child t).

Is p \perp r \mid \emptyset (no conditioning set)?
Is p \perp r \mid \{s\}?
Is p \perp t \mid \{r\}?

For each, name the only path between the two nodes, identify the junction type(s) on it, and apply the Bayes Ball rules.






TipWorked solution





This uses Week 2, The Bayes Ball algorithm.
1. p \perp r \mid \emptyset. The only path between p and r is p \to q \leftarrow r. Here q is a collider. With C=\emptyset, neither q nor any descendant of q (that is, s) is in C, so the collider is blocked. The one path is blocked, so p \perp r \mid \emptyset.
2. p \perp r \mid \{s\}. Same path, p \to q \leftarrow r, same collider q. Now C=\{s\}, and s is a descendant of the collider q (via q \to s), so the collider is open: shading a descendant of a collider opens it, exactly the explaining-away rule. The path is active, so p \not\perp r \mid \{s\}. Conditioning on s, which is not even on the direct route between p and r, is what creates the dependency, the same pattern as the lecture’s c-shaded example.
3. p \perp t \mid \{r\}. The only path between p and t is p \to q \leftarrow r \to t. There are two junctions: q is a collider (parents p,r), and r is a fork on this path (edges r\to q and r\to t both point out of r). With C=\{r\}: at the fork r, r is shaded, so the fork is blocked. That already blocks the whole path regardless of q (checking anyway: at the collider q, neither q nor its descendant s is in C=\{r\}, so q is also blocked). So p \perp t \mid \{r\}.
Answer. (1) p\perp r\mid\emptyset: yes. (2) p\perp r\mid\{s\}: no. (3) p\perp t\mid\{r\}: yes.

section: Problem 8: Why does Naive Bayes save so many parameters?
text:
Problem 8: Why does Naive Bayes save so many parameters?
A grocer wants to classify fruit as ripe (C=1) or unripe (C=0) from three binary features: color (X_1: red/green), softness (X_2: soft/firm), and smell (X_3: fragrant/faint). A Naive Bayes model assumes X_1, X_2, X_3 are conditionally independent given the ripeness label C.
Without computing any specific numbers, explain: (a) which of the lecture’s three canonical structures this independence assumption corresponds to, and why; (b) in general terms, why the assumption shrinks the parameter count from exponential in the number of features to linear in the number of features. (The exact MLE formulas for \hat\pi and \hat\theta_{jc} are left to work through with real counts on your own data; this problem is about the structural reason for the saving, not the computed values.)






TipWorked solution





This uses Week 2, Naive Bayes as a graphical model and Directed graphical models.
(a) Which structure. The assumption X_i \perp X_j \mid C for every feature pair is the common-cause structure repeated across every pair of features, with the ripeness label C playing the role of the shared cause. Each feature is an effect of C (color, softness, and smell are all downstream of whether the fruit is actually ripe), and once C is known, no feature carries extra information about any other feature. This is exactly the deadline example and Problem 6’s sensor example, generalized from one shared cause and two effects to one shared cause and d effects.
(b) Why the parameter count shrinks. Without any independence assumption, the DAG on C, X_1, X_2, X_3 is fully connected in the chain-rule order C,X_1,X_2,X_3: the i-th feature’s CPT conditions on C and every feature before it, so its table size doubles with each additional feature, giving a total that grows as 2^{d+1}-1 in the number of features d (Free parameters and the cost of the full joint, Why factor the joint). Removing every edge between features and keeping only the edges from C means each feature’s CPT now conditions on C alone, a table of fixed size regardless of how many other features exist. Summing a fixed-size table once per feature gives a total that grows linearly in d instead of exponentially. The structural reason is the same one from Directed graphical models: restricting how many parents a node can have is what buys the saving, and Naive Bayes pushes every feature’s parent set down to just \{C\}, the most aggressive restriction available short of assuming no dependence on C at all.
Answer. (a) Common cause, with C as the shared parent of every feature. (b) Fully connected costs grow exponentially in the number of features because each new feature’s CPT can condition on every earlier feature; capping every feature’s parent set at \{C\} makes each CPT a fixed size, so the total grows linearly instead.

title: Week 3: Markov Random Fields and Exact Inference
text:
From DAGs to undirected graphs
Overview. Week 2 built directed graphical models: pick an ordering of the variables, draw an arrow from each parent to each child, and read conditional independencies off the arrows. That works well when there is a natural causal or generative ordering, but many domains (a social network, a protein interaction network, the pixels of an image) have no natural direction to assign to an edge. This lecture introduces Markov random fields (MRFs), undirected graphical models where an edge means “these two variables interact” rather than “one causes the other.” We show what MRFs can express that DAGs cannot, and vice versa, then specialize to two concrete families: the Ising model (for discrete/binary variables) and Gaussian graphical models (for continuous ones), the latter directly useful for this course’s first assignment. The second half turns to exact inference: given a graphical model, how do we actually compute a marginal or conditional probability without enumerating every possible assignment? Variable elimination answers this for both DAGs and MRFs at once, and we finish with a worked example and a modern application, the restricted Boltzmann machine.
Skipped: the title slide and the assignment/office-hours announcements on slide 2 (the content summary from that same slide becomes the paragraph above).
Recall the Markov blanket of a variable X_i: the smallest set of other variables that makes X_i conditionally independent of everything else. In a DAG, the Markov blanket of X_i is its parents, its children, and its children’s other parents (the co-parents), because of the explaining-away effect from Week 2 (Conditional independence: three canonical structures in Week 2): observing a child can create dependence between that child’s parents.
This has an awkward consequence. Take a grid of variables X_1,\dots,X_{20} arranged in rows, where intuitively each variable should depend only on its four grid neighbors (up, down, left, right). If we try to encode this as a DAG by choosing some ordering of the variables (say, left to right, top to bottom) and drawing arrows accordingly, the Markov blanket of an interior node like X_8 can end up including nodes that have nothing to do with X_8’s grid neighbors. For example, X_8’s co-parents in one such DAG turn out to include X_4 and X_{12}, even though those are not grid-adjacent to X_8 at all, only because they happen to share a child with X_8 under the chosen edge orientation. The DAG is not wrong: it does encode a valid factorization. But its dependency structure does not match the “each cell depends on its neighbors” structure we actually wanted to express, and no choice of edge directions fixes this in general.
Figure 1. In the grid, X_8’s only neighbors are X_3, X_7, X_9, X_{13} (solid edges). X_4 and X_{12} (dashed outlines, no edge to X_8) are not grid-adjacent to X_8, yet a particular DAG encoding of this grid places them in X_8’s Markov blanket anyway.

title: Week 3: Markov Random Fields and Exact Inference
section: Markov random fields, cliques, and the factorization theorem
text:
Markov random fields, cliques, and the factorization theorem

Definition. An undirected graphical model, or Markov random field (MRF), represents a set of random variables as nodes of an undirected graph G, where an edge between two nodes means those variables interact directly, rather than one causing the other.

To write down what distributions an MRF represents, we need the notion of a clique.

Definition. A clique is a subset of nodes in which every pair is connected by an edge. A maximal clique is a clique that cannot be extended by adding one more adjacent node without breaking the all-pairs-connected property.


Definition. Let \boldsymbol{x} = (x_1,\dots,x_m) be all the variables in graph G, and let \mathcal{C} be the set of all maximal cliques of G. A distribution p factorizes with respect to G if p(\boldsymbol{x}) \propto \prod_{C \in \mathcal{C}} \psi_C(x_C) for some nonnegative potential functions \psi_C, where x_C = (x_i)_{i \in C}. The MRF on G represents exactly the distributions that factorize with respect to G.

Unlike a DAG’s conditional probability tables, a potential \psi_C need not sum or integrate to 1, and need not have any probabilistic interpretation on its own; it is simply a nonnegative score attached to each joint setting of the clique’s variables. The product of all the potentials is only proportional to p(\boldsymbol{x}), so an explicit normalizing constant Z = \sum_{\boldsymbol{x}} \prod_{C} \psi_C(x_C) (the partition function) is needed to turn it into an actual probability. This factored structure is what makes sums and integrals over p(\boldsymbol{x}) tractable: instead of manipulating one giant table over all variables jointly, we manipulate several small tables, one per clique, exactly the same motivation that drove the chain-rule factorization of Week 2 (Why factor the joint in Week 2).
As a small concrete instance, a 4-cycle of binary variables x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4 (edges 1\text{-}2, 2\text{-}3, 3\text{-}4, 4\text{-}1) has four maximal cliques, one per edge, so
p(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4) = \frac{1}{Z}\,\psi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2)\,\psi_{2,3}(x_2,x_3)\,\psi_{3,4}(x_3,x4)\,\psi_{1,4}(x_1,x_4).

title: Week 3: Markov Random Fields and Exact Inference
text:
The Hammersley-Clifford theorem
The factorization theorem above starts from a factored form and asks what independencies it implies. The Hammersley-Clifford theorem says the two directions coincide.

Hammersley-Clifford theorem. If p(\boldsymbol{x}) > 0 for all \boldsymbol{x}, the following are equivalent:

p factorizes with respect to G, i.e. p(\boldsymbol{x}) \propto \prod_{C \in \mathcal{C}} \psi_C(x_C) for nonnegative potentials \psi_C.
Global Markov property: X_A \perp X_B \mid X_S whenever S separates A from B in G (every path from A to B passes through S).


Two special cases of the global Markov property are worth naming directly, since they recur constantly: if i and j are not joined by an edge, then X_i \perp X_j \mid X_{\text{rest}} (conditioning on every other variable separates any two non-adjacent nodes); and the Markov blanket of X_i in an MRF is simply its graph neighbors, no co-parent correction needed, in contrast to the DAG case of From DAGs to undirected graphs.
Why the two directions match: a chain. The core mechanism is easiest to see on a three-node chain X-Y-Z, whose only maximal cliques are the edges \{X,Y\} and \{Y,Z\}, so the class of distributions that factorizes with respect to this graph is exactly those of the form f(x,y,z) = \alpha(x,y)\,\beta(y,z) for positive functions \alpha,\beta. The claim is that this is equivalent to X \perp Z \mid Y.
Factorized \Rightarrow independent. Using the product rule, f(x,y,z) = f(y,z)\,f(x\mid y,z), and separately f(x,y,z) = f(x\mid y)\,f(y,z) whenever X\perp Z\mid Y already holds, so a factorization of the stated form is available with \alpha(x,y) = f(x\mid y) and \beta(y,z) = f(y,z). This direction just restates the definition of conditional independence as a factorization.
Factorized \Rightarrow independent, without assuming it first. Start only from f(x,y,z)=\alpha(x,y)\beta(y,z) and derive the independence. Summing out x, f(y,z) = \Big(\sum_x \alpha(x,y)\Big)\beta(y,z). Dividing the joint by this marginal gives the conditional: f(x\mid y,z) = \frac{\alpha(x,y)\,\beta(y,z)}{\left(\sum_x \alpha(x,y)\right)\beta(y,z)} = \frac{\alpha(x,y)}{\sum_x \alpha(x,y)}. The right-hand side has no z in it at all, so f(x\mid y,z) does not depend on z, which is exactly X\perp Z\mid Y. The mechanism is the same cancellation that made Week 2’s regression decomposition work (Loss functions for regression in Week 2): a shared factor in numerator and denominator drops out, leaving no trace of the conditioned-out variable.

How many maximal cliques are there? Checking every pairwise connection within each candidate set gives five maximal cliques: \{1,2,3\}, \{2,3,5\}, \{2,4,5\}, \{3,5,6\}, and \{4,5,6,7\}. Node 5 belongs to four of the five, since it connects to nearly every other node; that is exactly why it appears in so many of the clique’s variable lists below.
What is the factorization? p(\boldsymbol{x}) \propto \psi_{1,2,3}(x_1,x_2,x_3)\,\psi_{2,3,5}(x_2,x_3,x_5)\,\psi_{2,4,5}(x_2,x_4,x_5) {}\times \psi_{3,5,6}(x_3,x_5,x_6)\,\psi_{4,5,6,7}(x_4,x_5,x_6,x_7).
What independencies does the graph imply? Reading the global Markov property off the picture: the set \{4,5,6,7\} separates \{1,2\} from nothing directly, but removing \{3,4,5\} disconnects \{1,2\} from \{6,7\} entirely (every path from 1 or 2 to 6 or 7 passes through 3, 4, or 5), so (X_1,X_2) \perp (X_6,X_7) \mid (X_3,X_4,X_5). Similarly, node 5 is the only path connecting 1 to 5’s other neighbors that does not already pass through 2 or 3; more simply, every path from 1 to 5 passes through 2 or 3, so X_1 \perp X_5 \mid (X_2,X_3).






Note



Practice question. In Figure 3, is X_1 \perp X_4 \mid X_2? Check by finding every path from node 1 to node 4 and seeing whether \{2\} blocks all of them.
Solution. Node 1’s only edges go to nodes 2 and 3, so every path out of node 1 starts by visiting 2 or 3. A path starting 1\to 2 \to 4 is blocked once we condition on \{2\}, since 2 is on that path and is now fixed. But a path starting 1\to 3 \to 5 \to 4 never touches node 2 at all, so conditioning on \{2\} does nothing to it: it stays open. Since at least one path from 1 to 4 survives, \{2\} does not separate them, so X_1 \not\perp X_4 \mid X_2. Separating 1 from 4 would require conditioning on a set that intersects every route out of node 1’s second neighbor, node 3, as well, for example \{2,3\} or \{3,5\}.

What MRFs can express that DAGs cannot, and vice versa
The two representations are not nested: each can express independence patterns the other cannot.
An MRF with no equivalent DAG. Take the 4-cycle A-D-B-C-A shown below (edges A\text{-}D, A\text{-}B, D\text{-}C, B\text{-}C, and no diagonal). Its two maximal cliques give two independence statements simultaneously: A \perp C \mid \{D,B\} and B \perp D \mid \{A,C\}. Any attempt to encode this as a DAG by orienting the four edges necessarily creates a v-structure (a collider) at one of the four nodes, and by the explaining-away logic of Week 2, that collider blocks one of the two independencies while leaving the other intact, or introduces an independence (such as making B and D marginally independent) that was never true in the undirected model. title: Week 3: Markov Random Fields and Exact Inference
text:
MRFs as exponential families






Note



Homework-relevant. This section’s log-linear form and sufficient statistics are the same exponential-family machinery from Week 1 (Maximum likelihood estimation in Week 1), applied to potentials instead of a single density. If a current or upcoming assignment asks you to write an MRF or a Gaussian graphical model in exponential-family form, this derivation pattern is the one to reuse.


Consider the parametric family p(\boldsymbol{x}\mid\theta) = \frac{1}{Z(\theta)}\prod_{C\in\mathcal{C}} \psi_C(x_C\mid\theta_C), \qquad \theta = (\theta_C)_{C\in\mathcal{C}}. Taking the log of the product turns it into a sum, exactly as in Week 1’s move from likelihood to log-likelihood: p(\boldsymbol{x}\mid\theta) = \exp\Big\{\sum_{C\in\mathcal{C}} \log\psi_C(x_C\mid\theta_C) - \underbrace{\log Z(\theta)}_{=A(\theta)}\Big\}. If each potential has a log-linear form, \log\psi_C(x_C\mid\theta_C) = \theta_C^\top \phi_C(x_C), this becomes exactly Week 1’s exponential family, with natural parameter \theta, sufficient statistic \phi = (\phi_C)_{C\in\mathcal{C}}, and log-partition function A(\theta) = \log Z(\theta): p(\boldsymbol{x}\mid\theta) = \exp\Big\{\sum_{C\in\mathcal{C}} \theta_C^\top \phi_C(x_C) - A(\theta)\Big\}.
When does the log-linear form hold? For finite discrete x_C, \log\psi_C takes only finitely many values, one per setting of x_C. Let \theta_C list all those values, and let \phi_C(x_C) be the indicator vector with a 1 in the entry matching x_C’s current setting and 0 elsewhere: then \theta_C^\top \phi_C(x_C) just selects out the one matching entry, which is \log\psi_C(x_C\mid\theta_C) by construction. As in Week 1’s exponential-family facts, the log-partition function’s gradient recovers an expectation: \partial \log Z(\theta) / \partial \theta_C = \mathbb{E}[\phi_C(X_C)].
Worked example: minimal vs. non-minimal. Take the chain X_1 - X_2 - X_3 with binary variables, so p(x_1,x_2,x_3\mid\theta) = \frac{1}{Z(\theta)}\psi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2\mid\theta_{1,2})\,\psi_{2,3}(x_2,x_3\mid\theta_{2,3}). Following the finite-discrete construction, index \theta_{1,2} by the four settings of (x_1,x_2): \theta_{1,2} := \begin{bmatrix}\log\psi_{1,2}(0,0)\\ \log\psi_{1,2}(0,1)\\ \log\psi_{1,2}(1,0)\\ \log\psi_{1,2}(1,1)\end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^4, with \phi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2) the corresponding indicator vector, e.g. \phi_{1,2}(0,1) = (0,1,0,0)^\top. This reproduces \log\psi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2\mid\theta_{1,2}) = \theta_{1,2}^\top \phi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2) exactly, and the resulting family has Z(\theta) = 1 by construction.
But this representation is not minimal: every setting of \phi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2) has entries summing to exactly 1 (only one indicator is ever “on”), so all four possible values of \phi_{1,2} lie on the hyperplane \{v : v^\top(1,1,1,1)^\top = 1\} rather than spanning \mathbb{R}^4. A non-minimal exponential family fails the usual gradient identity (\nabla A(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_\theta[\phi(X)] does not hold as stated here, since A(\theta)=0 identically in this parameterization). The fix is to drop the redundant first coordinate and re-express the other three relative to it: \bar\theta_{1,2} = \big(\theta^{(1)},\,\theta^{(2)},\,\theta^{(3)}\big), \quad \text{where} \theta^{(1)} = \log\psi_{1,2}(0,1)-\log\psi_{1,2}(0,0), \theta^{(2)} = \log\psi_{1,2}(1,0)-\log\psi_{1,2}(0,0), \theta^{(3)} = \log\psi_{1,2}(1,1)-\log\psi_{1,2}(0,0), \bar\phi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2) = \begin{bmatrix}(1-x_1)x_2\\ x_1(1-x_2)\\ x_1 x_2\end{bmatrix}, and analogously for \bar\theta_{2,3}, \bar\phi_{2,3}. This three-dimensional-per-edge parameterization is minimal, and its log-partition function, A(\bar\theta) = \log\psi_{1,2}(0,0)\,\psi_{2,3}(0,0), is no longer identically zero. The general lesson: writing every table entry as its own parameter is always possible but wastes one degree of freedom per clique to the normalization constraint; a minimal representation fixes a reference setting (here, (0,0)) and parameterizes only the contrast with it.

title: Week 3: Markov Random Fields and Exact Inference
text:
The Ising model

Definition. The Ising model is an MRF over spin variables x_s \in \{-1,+1\}, originally used to model magnets, with pairwise clique potentials \psi_{st}(x_s,x_t) = e^{J_{st}\,x_s x_t}, where J_{st} is the coupling strength between neighboring nodes s and t (J_{st}=0 if s,t are not connected).

Since x_s x_t = +1 when the two spins agree and -1 when they disagree, \psi_{st}(-1,-1)=\psi_{st}(1,1)=e^{J_{st}} while \psi_{st}(-1,1)=\psi_{st}(1,-1)=e^{-J_{st}}: a positive coupling J_{st}>0 makes the potential larger when the two spins agree, so the model favors, but does not force, matching neighbors. Adding a per-node potential \psi_s(x_s) = e^{b_s x_s} (an external field biasing each spin individually) gives the overall distribution p(\boldsymbol{x}) \propto \prod_{s\sim t} \psi_{st}(x_s,x_t) \prod_s \psi_s(x_s) = \exp\Big\{\sum_{s\sim t} J_{st}x_sx_t + \sum_s b_s x_s\Big\}, where s\sim t ranges over edges. This is exactly the log-linear exponential family of MRFs as exponential families, with sufficient statistics x_sx_t per edge and x_s per node. By Hammersley-Clifford, setting J_{st}=0 for a non-edge pair is precisely what makes X_s \perp X_t \mid X_{\text{rest}}.






Note



Practice question. In an Ising model with three spins X_1,X_2,X_3 arranged in the chain X_1-X_2-X_3 (so J_{13}=0), is X_1 \perp X_3 marginally (with X_2 unobserved), or only X_1 \perp X_3 \mid X_2?
Solution. J_{13}=0 says only that X_1 and X_3 are not directly coupled, which by Hammersley-Clifford gives the conditional statement X_1 \perp X_3 \mid X_2 (they are the two endpoints of a chain, and X_2 is the sole separator between them, exactly the causal-chain structure of Week 2’s Conditional independence: three canonical structures). It says nothing about the marginal relationship: both spins are still coupled to the same neighbor X_2, so marginally (summing X_2 out) X_1 and X_3 are typically dependent, the common-cause pattern from the same Week 2 section. This is the Ising-model instance of the general chain fact proved in The Hammersley-Clifford theorem.

title: Week 3: Markov Random Fields and Exact Inference
text:
Gaussian graphical models
MRFs are not limited to discrete variables. For continuous variables, the multivariate Gaussian gives a graphical model whose edges correspond directly to nonzero entries of a matrix.
Recall the multivariate normal: for X=(X_1,\dots,X_m), mean vector \mu\in\mathbb{R}^m, and a symmetric positive definite covariance matrix \Sigma (meaning u^\top \Sigma u > 0 for every nonzero u), we write X\sim N_m(\mu,\Sigma) if f(\boldsymbol{x};\mu,\Sigma) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{m/2}(\det\Sigma)^{1/2}} \times\exp\!\left(-\tfrac{1}{2}(\boldsymbol{x}-\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\boldsymbol{x}-\mu)\right), with \mathbb{E}[X]=\mu and \mathrm{var}(X)=\Sigma. Splitting X into two blocks X=(X_A,X_B) with \mu=(\mu_A,\mu_B) and \Sigma = \begin{bmatrix}\Sigma_{AA} & \Sigma_{AB}\\ \Sigma_{BA} & \Sigma_{BB}\end{bmatrix}, the marginal is again Gaussian, X_A \sim N(\mu_A,\Sigma_{AA}), and the conditional is X_A \mid X_B=x_B \sim N\big(\mu_A + \Sigma_{AB}\Sigma_{BB}^{-1}(x_B-\mu_B),\; \Sigma_{AA}-\Sigma_{AB}\Sigma_{BB}^{-1}\Sigma_{BA}\big), where the conditional covariance does not depend on the observed value x_B, only on which variables were observed.
Reading independence off \Sigma. Marginal independence is simple: X_i \perp X_j if and only if \Sigma_{ij}=0. Conditioning on everything else is more useful for graphical models, and it is governed not by \Sigma but by its inverse. Let K = \Sigma^{-1}, the precision matrix. Writing R = V\setminus\{i,j\} for every other variable, the following are equivalent: X_i \perp X_j \mid X_R; \Sigma_{ij} - \Sigma_{i,R}\Sigma_{R,R}^{-1}\Sigma_{R,j} = 0; and (\Sigma^{-1})_{ij} = K_{ij} = 0. The last equivalence is the useful one: a single entry of the precision matrix tells us whether two variables are conditionally independent given everything else, with no matrix inversion needed per pair.

Definition. A Gaussian graphical model represents X\sim N(\mu,\Sigma) with precision matrix K=\Sigma^{-1} as an undirected graph on the coordinates of X, with an edge between i and j exactly when K_{ij}\neq 0. Writing out the density in terms of K, p(\boldsymbol{x}\mid\mu,\Sigma) \propto \prod_s e^{-\frac{1}{2}K_{ss}(x_s-\mu_s)^2} \prod_{s<t} e^{-K_{st}(x_s-\mu_s)(x_t-\mu_t)}, so K_{ij}=0 if and only if X_i \perp X_j \mid X_{\text{rest}}, matching the Hammersley-Clifford statement of The Hammersley-Clifford theorem.

Practice question. For the precision matrix in Figure 6, is X_1 \perp X_3? Is X_1 \perp X_3 \mid X_2?
Solution. Marginal independence is governed by \Sigma, not K, so the zero pattern of K alone does not answer the first question; in general \Sigma_{13}\neq 0 even though K_{13}=0, since matrix inversion mixes entries. For the conditional question, K_{13}=0 directly gives X_1 \perp X_3 \mid X_{\text{rest}} = X_1 \perp X_3 \mid \{X_2,X_4,X_5\}, conditioning on every other variable, not just X_2. Whether X_1\perp X_3\mid X_2 alone holds is a separate, graph-separation question: in the 5-cycle, removing only node 2 leaves a path 1-5-4-3 still connecting 1 and 3, so \{2\} does not separate them and X_1\not\perp X_3\mid X_2 in general.








Note



Homework-relevant. Fitting a Gaussian graphical model by maximum likelihood is a direct continuous-variable analogue of Week 1’s Bernoulli MLE (Maximum likelihood estimation in Week 1): same “write the log-likelihood, then optimize” pattern, different sufficient statistic.


Suppose we observe i.i.d. data \boldsymbol{x}_{1:n} = \{\boldsymbol{x}_1,\dots,\boldsymbol{x}_n\} from an m-variate Gaussian with (for simplicity, after centering the data) mean zero, and write K=\Sigma^{-1}. The log-density is \log f(\boldsymbol{x}; K) = -\tfrac{m}{2}\log(2\pi) + \tfrac{1}{2}\log\det K - \tfrac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{x}^\top K \boldsymbol{x}. Dropping the constant that does not involve K, the log-likelihood over n points is \ell_n(K;\boldsymbol{x}_{1:n}) = \frac{n}{2}\log\det(K) - \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^n \boldsymbol{x}_i^\top K \boldsymbol{x}_i. The sum simplifies using the trace identity u^\top K u = \mathrm{tr}(Kuu^\top) and linearity of trace: \sum_{i=1}^n \boldsymbol{x}_i^\top K \boldsymbol{x}_i = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathrm{tr}(K\boldsymbol{x}_i\boldsymbol{x}_i^\top) = n\,\mathrm{tr}(K S_n), S_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \boldsymbol{x}_i \boldsymbol{x}_i^\top, where S_n is the sample covariance matrix, playing the same role here that the sample mean played in Week 1’s Bernoulli MLE: it is the sufficient statistic that summarizes all n data points for the purpose of estimating K. Substituting back, \ell_n(K;\boldsymbol{x}_{1:n}) = \frac{n}{2}\big(\log\det(K) - \mathrm{tr}(KS_n)\big). Two facts about this objective, useful for actually solving the maximization: \log\det(K) is a strictly concave function of K, so the objective has a unique maximizer, and \mathrm{tr}(KS_n) is linear in K. Their gradients are \nabla \log\det(K) = K^{-1} and \nabla\, \mathrm{tr}(KS_n) = S_n, so setting the gradient of \ell_n to zero gives K^{-1} = S_n, i.e. the maximum likelihood estimate of the covariance matrix is simply the sample covariance matrix, and \hat K_{\text{MLE}} = S_n^{-1}: the same “set the derivative to zero, read off an empirical average” pattern as every MLE derivation so far this course, just with a matrix-valued statistic in place of a scalar one.

title: Week 3: Markov Random Fields and Exact Inference
section: Exact inference as a conditional distribution
text:
Exact inference as a conditional distribution
Having built up two families of graphical models (DAGs in Week 2, MRFs in this lecture), we now ask a computational question common to both: given the model, how do we compute an actual number?

Definition. In a graphical model over \boldsymbol{x}, split the variables into x_E (the observed evidence), x_F (the unobserved variable(s) we want to infer), and x_R = \boldsymbol{x} - \{x_F,x_E\} (remaining variables, summed out). Inference is computing the conditional distribution p(x_F\mid x_E) = \frac{p(x_F,x_E)}{p(x_E)} = \frac{p(x_F,x_E)}{\sum_{x_F} p(x_F,x_E)}, where the joint over the subject of inference and the evidence is obtained by marginalizing out the remaining variables, p(x_F,x_E) = \sum_{x_R} p(x_F,x_E,x_R).

Both the numerator and the normalizing sum over x_F require summing over x_R (and, for the denominator, over x_F too), so the real computational question is how to perform these sums efficiently, which is exactly what variable elimination addresses.

title: Week 3: Markov Random Fields and Exact Inference
text:
Variable elimination
The order in which we marginalize out variables changes the computational cost dramatically, even though the final answer is the same regardless of order (summation commutes). Variable elimination is a simple, general exact-inference algorithm that applies to any graphical model, DAG or MRF, whose computational complexity depends on the graph structure and the chosen elimination order; it is a form of dynamic programming that avoids enumerating every joint assignment.
Worked example: a simple chain. Consider A\to B\to C\to D, and suppose we want the marginal p(D) with no evidence, so x_F=\{D\}, x_E=\{\}, x_R=\{A,B,C\}. Week 2’s chain rule gives p(A,B,C,D) = p(A)p(B\mid A)p(C\mid B)p(D\mid C).


  
    
      
    
  
  A simple chain
  
  
  
  
  A

Figure 7. A chain of four variables, used to compare naive marginalization against variable elimination.
Assume each variable takes k possible values. Marginalizing naively, p(D) = \sum_{A,B,C} p(A,B,C,D) = \sum_C \sum_B \sum_A p(A)p(B\mid A)p(C\mid B)p(D\mid C), costs O(k^4): every joint assignment of the four variables must be visited. Instead, choose an elimination order and push each sum as far inward as it will go, past every factor that does not mention the variable being summed: p(D) = \sum_C p(D\mid C) \left(\sum_B p(C\mid B) \sum_A p(A)p(B\mid A)\right). Working from the inside out, the innermost sum depends only on B once A is gone: \sum_A p(A)p(B\mid A) = p(B). Substituting back and repeating the same move for B: \sum_B p(C\mid B)\,p(B) = p(C). So the whole expression collapses to p(D) = \sum_C p(D\mid C)\,p(C). Every intermediate sum here touches at most two variables at once (k^2 terms), and there are n such sums, so the total cost is O(nk^2), compared to O(k^n) for constructing and marginalizing the full joint table directly: an exponential-to-polynomial improvement from exactly the same reordering trick that made Week 2’s chain-rule factorization efficient (Why factor the joint in Week 2).
Elimination ordering matters, and finding the best one is hard. The complexity of variable elimination depends on the chosen order, since different orders leave different numbers of variables inside each intermediate sum. Unfortunately, finding the elimination ordering that minimizes the worst intermediate sum is NP-hard in general, so in practice orderings are chosen by heuristics (or, in this course, simply given).

section: Sum-product inference: unifying DAGMs and MRFs
text:
Sum-product inference: unifying DAGMs and MRFs
Variable elimination on a DAG is really the same algorithm as on an MRF, once we notice that a DAG’s conditional probability tables are themselves just a special kind of nonnegative potential. Introduce a nonnegative factor \phi for each conditional probability table (or each MRF potential): for a DAG on X,A,B,C with p(A,B,C) = \sum_X p(X)p(A\mid X)p(B\mid A)p(C\mid B,X), write \phi_1(X)=p(X), \phi_2(A,X)=p(A\mid X), \phi_3(A,B)=p(B\mid A), \phi_4(X,B,C)=p(C\mid B,X), so p(A,B,C) = \sum_X \phi_1(X)\phi_2(A,X)\phi_3(A,B)\phi_4(X,B,C). The factor \phi_3(A,B) does not involve X, so it can be pulled outside the sum over X: p(A,B,C) = \phi_3(A,B) \sum_X \phi_1(X)\phi_2(A,X)\phi_4(X,B,C) = \phi_3(A,B)\,\tau(A,B,C). Marginalizing out X produces a brand new factor \tau(A,B,C), an intermediate factor that generally is not any original conditional probability table; it is simply whatever function of the remaining variables the sum happened to produce. This is the mechanical step that repeats at every stage of variable elimination.
Abstractly, both DAG and MRF inference reduce to the same sum-product computation: ::: {.boxed-eq} p(x_F\mid x_E) \propto \tau(x_F,x_E) = \sum_{x_R} \prod_{C\in\mathcal{F}} \psi_C(x_C), ::: where \mathcal{F} is the set of factors: for a DAG, \mathcal{F} consists of the sets \{i\}\cup\text{parents}(i) for every node i (one factor per conditional probability table); for an MRF, \mathcal{F} is the set of maximal cliques.

This graph gives the factorization p(C,D,I,G,S,L,H,J) = p(C)p(D\mid C)p(I)\,p(G\mid D,I)p(L\mid G)p(S\mid I)p(J\mid S,L)p(H\mid J,G). Reading off one factor per node (its own conditional probability table), \mathcal{F} = \big\{\{C\},\{C,D\},\{I\},\{G,D,I\},\{L,G\},\{S,I\},\{J,S,L\},\{H,J,G\}\big\}, so m=|\mathcal{F}|=8.
Suppose we want p(J), the probability of getting a job, with the elimination order C,D,I,H,G,S,L (an ordering the instructor supplies; finding an optimal one is the NP-hard problem from Variable elimination). Eliminate C first: it appears only in \psi(C) and \psi(C,D), so \sum_C \psi(C)\,\psi(C,D) = \tau(D). Eliminate D next, in \psi(G,D,I) and the new \tau(D): \sum_D \psi(G,D,I)\,\tau(D) = \tau(G,I). Eliminate I, in \psi(S,I), \psi(I), and \tau(G,I): \sum_I \psi(S,I)\,\psi(I)\,\tau(G,I) = \tau(S,G). Eliminate H, which appears only in \psi(H,G,J): \sum_H \psi(H,G,J) = \tau(G,J). Eliminate G, now present in \psi(L,G), \tau(S,G), and \tau(G,J): \sum_G \psi(L,G)\,\tau(S,G)\,\tau(G,J) = \tau(J,L,S). Eliminate S, in \psi(J,L,S) and \tau(J,L,S): \sum_S \psi(J,L,S)\,\tau(J,L,S) = \tau(J,L). Finally eliminate L: \sum_L \tau(J,L) = \tau(J). The result, \tau(J), is proportional to p(J); since Z=1 for a DAG’s own conditional probability tables (they are already properly normalized), no further rescaling is needed here, though for a general MRF the final \tau would still require dividing by \sum_{x_F}\tau(x_F) to become an actual probability.
Reading off the complexity. Each sum above is labeled by how many variables appear inside it: \sum_C has N_C=2 (namely C,D), \sum_D has N_D=3 (G,D,I), \sum_I has N_I=3 (S,I,G), \sum_H has N_H=3 (H,G,J), \sum_G has N_G=4 (L,G,S,J, the largest), \sum_S has N_S=3, and \sum_L has N_L=2. The complexity of variable elimination under a given ordering is O\big(m\,k^{N_{\max}}\big), \qquad N_{\max}=\max_i N_i, where m is the number of initial factors and k is the (assumed common) number of states per variable. Here N_{\max}=4 (achieved at the G-elimination step), so the cost of this particular ordering is O(8k^4): substantially better than enumerating the full 8-variable joint, but not as good as the chain example of Variable elimination, because this graph has a genuinely more complex dependency structure than a simple chain.

title: Week 3: Markov Random Fields and Exact Inference
text:
Variable elimination with evidence
The student-network example above had no observed evidence. Reintroducing evidence changes only which variable is fixed rather than summed.
Worked example. Take the DAG X_1 \to X_2 \to X_4, X_1 \to X_3 \to X_5 \to X_6, X_2 \to X_6 (so X_6 has two parents, X_2 and X_5), giving p(x_1,\dots,x_6) = p(x_1)p(x_2\mid x_1)p(x_3\mid x_1)p(x_4\mid x_2)p(x_5\mid x_3)p(x_6\mid x_2,x_5). Suppose X_6=\bar x_6 is observed and we want p(X_1\mid \bar x_6), so x_F=\{x_1\}, x_E=\{x_6\}, x_R=\{x_2,x_3,x_4,x_5\}. By the definition in Exact inference as a conditional distribution, p(x_1\mid \bar x_6) = \frac{p(x_1,\bar x_6)}{\sum_{x_1} p(x_1,\bar x_6)}. Computing the numerator by variable elimination in the order 2,3,4,5 (the observed value \bar x_6 is simply substituted into p(x_6\mid x_2,x_5) wherever it appears, rather than summed over): p(x_1,\bar x_6) = p(x_1)\sum_{x_2} p(x_2\mid x_1)\sum_{x_3} p(x_3\mid x_1)\sum_{x_4} p(x_4\mid x_2)\sum_{x_5} p(x_5\mid x_3)\,p(\bar x_6\mid x_2,x_5). The innermost sum over x_5 produces a new factor depending on x_2,x_3: \sum_{x_5} p(x_5\mid x_3)\,p(\bar x_6\mid x_2,x_5) = p(\bar x_6\mid x_2,x_3). The next sum, over x_4, involves only p(x_4\mid x_2), none of whose terms depend on x_4 after it is summed out (it sums to 1), so it drops out entirely: \sum_{x_4} p(x_4\mid x_2) = 1. This leaves p(x_1,\bar x_6) = p(x_1)\sum_{x_2} p(x_2\mid x_1)\sum_{x_3} p(x_3\mid x_1)\,p(\bar x_6\mid x_2,x_3). Summing x_3 next produces p(\bar x_6\mid x_1,x_2) (using \sum_{x_3}p(x_3\mid x_1)\,p(\bar x_6\mid x_2,x_3) = p(\bar x_6\mid x_1,x_2) by the product and sum rules), and then x_2: p(x_1,\bar x_6) = p(x_1)\sum_{x_2} p(x_2\mid x_1)\,p(\bar x_6\mid x_1,x_2) = p(x_1)\,p(\bar x_6\mid x_1). So the whole computation collapses to the two-factor product one would expect from a two-node chain X_1 \to X_6, even though the actual graph has six nodes; every other variable was marginalized away without ever touching a table larger than three variables at once. Normalizing gives the final answer: p(x_1\mid \bar x_6) = \frac{p(x_1)\,p(\bar x_6\mid x_1)}{\sum_{x_1} p(x_1)\,p(\bar x_6\mid x_1)}. This is Bayes’ rule from Week 1 (Worked example: a diagnostic test in Week 1), rederived as a special case of variable elimination: computing a posterior for a two-variable relationship, after algebraically marginalizing away every variable that connects them only indirectly.

title: Week 3: Markov Random Fields and Exact Inference
text:
Restricted Boltzmann machines
As a modern application tying together the Ising model, exponential families, and Hammersley-Clifford, consider a restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM): a special Ising model over visible variables X_1,\dots,X_k and hidden variables H_1,\dots,H_l, all in \{-1,+1\}, whose graph is bipartite: every H_i connects to every X_j, but no H_i-H_{i'} or X_j-X_{j'} edges exist at all.

Figure 9. An RBM’s graph: every hidden node connects to every visible node, and there are no hidden-hidden or visible-visible edges.
Writing the Ising-style distribution with per-edge potentials \psi_{X_i,H_j}(x_i,h_j) = \exp\{\frac{1}{l}\alpha_i x_i + \frac{1}{k}\beta_j h_j + J_{ij}x_ih_j\} (splitting the node biases evenly across the edges touching each node so that the product of edge potentials reproduces the full node bias), the joint is p(x_1,\dots,x_k,h_1,\dots,h_l) = \frac{1}{Z}\prod_{i=1}^k\prod_{j=1}^l \psi_{X_i,H_j}(x_i,h_j). Computing Z exactly can be expensive (it is a sum over all 2^{k+l} joint settings), but the bipartite structure lets us compute the two conditional distributions p(x\mid h) and p(h\mid x) efficiently, without ever needing Z. This is exactly what the Hammersley-Clifford theorem predicts: since there are no edges between different H_i’s, they are all mutually independent given X (every H_i-H_{i'} pair is separated by the fully-observed X, the same non-adjacent-pair rule from The Hammersley-Clifford theorem), so the joint conditional factors into a per-node product, and each factor can be computed on its own: p(h_j\mid x) = \frac{\prod_{i=1}^k \psi_{ij}(x_i,h_j)}{\prod_{i=1}^k\psi_{ij}(x_i,-1) + \prod_{i=1}^k\psi_{ij}(x_i,1)} = \sigma\Big(\beta_j + \sum_i J_{ij}x_i\Big), where \sigma(y) = \frac{e^y}{e^{-y}+e^y} = \frac{1}{1+e^{-2y}} is the sigmoid function. This is the origin of the sigmoid activation function used throughout neural networks: it is exactly the conditional-probability formula that falls out of treating a layer of binary units as conditionally independent given the layer below, under an Ising-style pairwise potential.

title: Week 3: Markov Random Fields and Exact Inference
text:
Summary






Note



Key takeaways from Week 3:

Markov random fields (MRFs) model undirected interactions: p(\boldsymbol{x}) \propto \prod_{C\in\mathcal{C}} \psi_C(x_C) over maximal cliques \mathcal{C}. The Hammersley-Clifford theorem says this factorization is equivalent to the global Markov property, X_A\perp X_B\mid X_S whenever S separates A from B in the graph.
MRFs and DAGs are not nested: a 4-cycle’s independencies cannot be captured by any DAG, and explaining-away cannot be captured by any MRF.
MRFs are exponential families when potentials are log-linear; a minimal representation drops one redundant coordinate per clique. The Ising model and Gaussian graphical models (where K_{ij}=0 \iff X_i\perp X_j\mid X_{\text{rest}} for the precision matrix K) are the two running examples, and Gaussian MLE reduces to \hat K^{-1}=S_n, the sample covariance.
Inference is computing p(x_F\mid x_E) by marginalizing out x_R. Variable elimination does this efficiently by choosing an order and pushing sums inward; the same sum-product algorithm handles DAGs and MRFs via a shared notion of factors, and the resulting intermediate factors (\tau) are what make the computation dynamic-programming-style rather than exponential.
Restricted Boltzmann machines are a bipartite Ising model where Hammersley-Clifford guarantees the hidden units are conditionally independent given the visible ones (and vice versa), giving the sigmoid activation as a direct consequence rather than an ad hoc choice.

title: Glossary
text:
Supervised / unsupervised / semi-supervised / reinforcement learning: the four standard ML problem settings, distinguished by what data or signal is available during learning (week 1, What is machine learning).
Discriminative model: a model of the conditional p(c\mid x) only, used directly for prediction (week 1, Discriminative vs generative).
Generative model: a model of the joint p(c,x), which can also generate new examples (week 1, Discriminative vs generative).
Joint distribution: the probability of every combination of outcomes of two or more random variables (week 1, Joint, marginal, and conditional).
Marginal distribution: the distribution of one variable, obtained by summing the joint over the others (week 1, Joint, marginal, and conditional).
Conditional distribution: the distribution of one variable given a fixed value of another; joint divided by marginal (week 1, Joint, marginal, and conditional).
Sensitivity / specificity / prevalence: the true-positive rate, true-negative rate, and prior probability of a condition, the three numbers that define a diagnostic-test model (week 1, diagnostic test).
Parametric model: a family of distributions \{p(x\mid\theta):\theta\in\Theta\} indexed by a parameter (week 1, Parametric models).
i.i.d.: independently and identically distributed; each data point drawn independently from the same distribution (week 1, Parametric models).
Likelihood function: the probability of the observed data, viewed as a function of the parameter (week 1, Parametric models).
Log-likelihood: the logarithm of the likelihood; a sum instead of a product, easier to optimize (week 1, Parametric models).
Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE): choosing the parameter value that maximizes the likelihood of the observed data (week 1, MLE).
Sufficient statistic: a summary of the data that captures everything relevant to estimating the parameter; formalized by the Fisher–Neyman factorization theorem (week 1, Sufficient statistics).
Exponential family: the class of distributions expressible as h(x)\exp\{\eta^\top T(x) - A(\eta)\}, unifying the Bernoulli, Multinomial, Gaussian, and many other named distributions (week 1, Exponential families).
Natural parameter (\eta): the parameter coordinate an exponential family is written in terms of; not always the same coordinate as the distribution’s usual parameters (week 1, Exponential families and Gaussian).
Log-partition function (A(\eta)): the normalizing term of an exponential family; its derivative gives the mean of the sufficient statistic (week 1, Exponential families and mean of sufficient statistics).
Carrying measure / base measure (h(x)): the part of an exponential-family density that does not depend on the parameter (week 1, Exponential families).
Log-odds: \log\frac{\theta}{1-\theta} (or, for more than two outcomes, \log(q_i/q_K) against a reference class); the natural parameter of the Bernoulli and Multinomial exponential families (week 1, Bernoulli and Multinomial).

title: Glossary
text:
Week 2

Decision region (\mathcal{R}_k): a subset of the input space assigned to class \mathcal{C}_k; the decision regions partition the input space (week 2, From inference to decision).
Loss function / loss matrix (L_{kj}): the cost of deciding class j when the true class is k; generalizes plain misclassification rate, which is the special case of a 0/1 loss matrix (week 2, Expected loss).
Expected loss: the loss matrix weighted by the joint, integrated over the chosen decision regions; minimizing it over regions gives the discriminant rule (week 2, Expected loss).
Discriminant rule: assign x to the class j minimizing \sum_k L_{kj}\,p(\mathcal{C}_k\mid x) (week 2, The discriminant rule and the reject option).
Reject option: declining to decide when every class posterior falls below a threshold \theta (week 2, The discriminant rule and the reject option).
Regression function (y(x)): a function approximating a continuous target t from input x; under squared loss, the loss-minimizing choice is y(x)=\mathbb{E}[t\mid x] (week 2, Loss functions for regression).
Directed acyclic graphical model (DAG) / Bayes net: a graph whose nodes are random variables and whose edges encode assumed direct dependence, inducing the factorization p(x_i\mid\text{parents}(x_i)) (week 2, Directed graphical models).
Conditional probability table (CPT): the table of parameters for p(x_i\mid\text{parents}(x_i)) at one node of a DAG; a binary node with K_i parents needs 2^{K_i} parameters (week 2, Directed graphical models).
D-separation: the graph-theoretic criterion for reading conditional independence x_A\perp x_B\mid x_C directly off a DAG (week 2, Bayes Ball algorithm).
Causal chain / common cause / explaining away: the three canonical three-node independence structures; conditioning on the middle node blocks dependence in the first two, and conditioning on a common effect (or its descendant) can create dependence in the third (week 2, Conditional independence: three canonical structures).
Bayes Ball algorithm: an algorithm that tests x_A\perp x_B\mid x_C by “bouncing” a ball from nodes in A along the graph, blocked or passed at each node per the chain/common-cause/common-effect rules (week 2, The Bayes Ball algorithm).
Naive Bayes: a classifier whose graphical model assumes every feature is conditionally independent of every other feature given the class label, a common-cause structure with the class as the shared parent (week 2, Naive Bayes as a graphical model).
Hidden Markov model (HMM): a graphical model with a Markov chain of unobserved states, each emitting an observed variable at every time step (week 2, DGMs in the wild).
Noisy-OR: a conditional probability table shape in which a child node is likely positive if any one of its parents is positive, used in medical-diagnosis networks such as Quick Medical Reference (week 2, DGMs in the wild).

title: Glossary
text:
Week 3

Markov random field (MRF): an undirected graphical model where an edge means two variables interact directly, rather than one causing the other (week 3, Markov random fields, cliques, and the factorization theorem).
Clique / maximal clique: a subset of nodes all pairwise connected by an edge; maximal if it cannot be extended by one more adjacent node (week 3, Markov random fields, cliques, and the factorization theorem).
Potential function (\psi_C): a nonnegative, not-necessarily-normalized score attached to a clique’s joint variable setting; the product of potentials over all maximal cliques is proportional to the MRF’s distribution (week 3, Markov random fields, cliques, and the factorization theorem).
Partition function (Z): the normalizing constant that turns a product of potentials into an actual probability distribution (week 3, Markov random fields, cliques, and the factorization theorem).
Hammersley-Clifford theorem: for a strictly positive distribution, factorizing with respect to a graph G is equivalent to the global Markov property on G (week 3, The Hammersley-Clifford theorem).
Global Markov property: X_A\perp X_B\mid X_S whenever S separates A from B in the graph (week 3, The Hammersley-Clifford theorem).
Ising model: an MRF over spin variables x_s\in\{-1,+1\} with pairwise potentials \psi_{st}(x_s,x_t)=e^{J_{st}x_sx_t}, used to model magnets (week 3, The Ising model).
Precision matrix (K=\Sigma^{-1}): the inverse covariance matrix of a multivariate Gaussian; K_{ij}=0 if and only if X_i\perp X_j\mid X_{\text{rest}} (week 3, Gaussian graphical models).
Gaussian graphical model: an undirected graph on the coordinates of a multivariate Gaussian, with an edge between i,j exactly when K_{ij}\neq 0 (week 3, Gaussian graphical models).
Sample covariance matrix (S_n): the sufficient statistic \frac{1}{n}\sum_i \boldsymbol{x}_i\boldsymbol{x}_i^\top for maximum likelihood estimation of a (mean-zero) Gaussian’s covariance; the MLE is \hat\Sigma_{\text{MLE}}=S_n (week 3, Gaussian graphical models).
Evidence / query / remaining variables (x_E, x_F, x_R): the observed, to-be-inferred, and marginalized-out variables in an inference query p(x_F\mid x_E) (week 3, Exact inference as a conditional distribution).
Variable elimination: an exact inference algorithm that computes marginals or conditionals by summing out variables one at a time in a chosen order, reusing intermediate sums rather than enumerating the full joint (week 3, Variable elimination).
Elimination ordering: the order in which variables are summed out during variable elimination; it determines the algorithm’s computational cost, and finding the optimal order is NP-hard (week 3, Variable elimination).
Intermediate factor (\tau): a new, generally non-probabilistic function of the remaining variables produced by summing out one variable during variable elimination (week 3, Sum-product inference: unifying DAGMs and MRFs).
Sum-product algorithm: the general inference computation \tau(x_F,x_E)=\sum_{x_R}\prod_{C\in\mathcal{F}}\psi_C(x_C) shared by DAGs (factors = node plus parents) and MRFs (factors = maximal cliques) (week 3, Sum-product inference: unifying DAGMs and MRFs).
Restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM): a bipartite Ising model over visible and hidden binary units, with no within-layer edges, whose hidden units are conditionally independent given the visible units by Hammersley-Clifford (week 3, Restricted Boltzmann machines).
